lines.text: A dimpled golf ball can fly nearly twice as far as a smooth one. How can little dents do that?
As a ball flies, air flows around it, then peels off the back, leaving a swirling, low pressure wake. That wake pulls the ball backward.
On a smooth ball, the air peels off early, so the wake is huge.
Dimples stir up a thin layer of turbulent air right at the surface. That turbulent layer clings to the ball longer.
So the air leaves later, the wake shrinks, and drag drops.
Add backspin, and the dimples help create lift, keeping the ball in the air longer.
Golfers discovered this by accident: old scuffed balls flew farther than new smooth ones.
